title: Rachael Li Ousts Alice Lee In Women's; Caruana, Liang Join 4-Way Lead
summary: Both tournaments are wide open after six decisive games on Thursday. Four players lead the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship: GM Wesley So, GM Andy Woodward, GM Fabiano Caruana, and GM Awonder Liang. Caruana scored a bounce-back win against GM Sam Shankland and Liang served GM Levon Aronian a second consecutive loss. So and Woodward, who started off in the lead, made draws with GMs Abhimanyu Mishra and Hans Niemann to maintain their positions. In the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship, WIM Rachael Li took down the leader IM Alice Lee to shake up the standings. Now there are three leaders: Li, Lee (despite the loss), and WGM Thalia Cervantes (who defeated IM Nazi Paikidze). We saw two more decisive results: IM Carissa Yip scored her first win against IM Anna Zatonskih and GM Irina Krush scored her third against IM Anna Sargsyan. Round seven is on Friday, October 16, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 6: Open Standings After Round 6: Women Round 6 Results: Open We are officially in the second half of the championships, and every player still has incentives to finish strong. There is a $5,000 prize in each event awarded to the players who have the strongest performance in rounds six through 11, regardless of their final standings. There were two decisive games in the open championship, which allowed Caruana and Liang to join the four-way tie for first. After a tough loss against Woodward the day before, Caruana is very much back in the running to defend his title—and if he does it this year, he will be the first to win five U.S. Championships in a row. His loss on Wednesday ended his unbeaten streak of 54 games in the U.S. Championship. He said, "I didn't play too well, and I was under pressure the whole game." Even though he had some chances to survive at the end, Caruana said that he would have had to sacrifice a piece. Nevertheless, he bounced back with a win against Shankland with the black pieces in the endgame arising from the Queen's Gambit Declined Magnus Variation. Neither player made any serious mistakes in the first 25 moves, but things turned dramatically after 26.Kd3?, and Caruana converted like a machine. The game lasted only 11 more moves.

title: FIDE World Junior U20 Rapid and Blitz Championships: Registration deadline extended
summary: FIDE, in cooperation with the United Arab Emirates Chess Federation and Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club, invites all FIDE member federations to participate in the World Junior U20 Rapid and Blitz Championships 2026. Each federation can register an unlimited number of players. The championships will be held in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates, from November 1 (arrival) to November 7 (departure), 2026. The winners of the World Junior Rapid & Blitz Championships 2025 and the top 10 players on the starting list (5 Rapid + 5 Blitz for the open section and 5 Rapid + 5 Blitz for the girls’ section) are entitled to free full-board accommodation in a double room. FIDE member Federations should proceed with the registration of their participants. Please note that eligible players must be born on or after January 1, 2006. The official registration link: https://juniorrapidandblitz2026.fide.com   Email: juniorrapidblitz@fide.com Invitation, regulations, schedule (PDF) The deadline for registration, hotel reservations and receipt of all applicable payments has been extended to October 27, 2026.

title: 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners: India wins double gold, Mexico triumphs in men’s section
summary: Mexico claimed title in the men’s category, while India earned double gold, winning women’s and youth sections.   The 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners concluded on October 15 with tightly contested finals in all three categories. Each final match consisted of two sets with colors reversed. Let’s have a look at how the action unfolded on the final day of the competition. Men’s section final: Mexico – Armenia (2-2 and 3-1) In the first set Mexico had white pieces on all boards but did not manage to capitalize on the first move advantage. Mexico scored wins on boards two and three, but Armenia struck back on boards one and four, and the set ended in a hard-fought draw 2-2.   Armenia had white in the second set, but somewhat surprisingly, it was all Mexico who prevailed on boards one, two and three in topsy-turvy games. Federal Social Rehabilitation Center number 18 (CEFERESO-18) Coahuila, Mexico, deservedly won the match and captured the title. Women’s section final: India – Mexico (4-0 and 4-0) It was a lopsided final as India (Government Children Home, Bhopal) swept Mexico (Federal Social Rehabilitation Center number 16 (CEFERESO-16) Morelos) in both sets to claim gold. Youth section final (2.5-1.5 and 2-2) The match was decided in the first set which India narrowly won by 2.5-1.5. In the second set Serbia pushed hard scoring victories on boards one and three, but Indian youngsters retaliated on boards two and four to draw the set and secure the title. This year’s championship, which allowed correctional facilities separated by thousands of kilometers to meet over the same chessboard, was a great success. The event established a new participation record, with 140 teams from 56 countries taking part. Organised by FIDE and the Cook County (Chicago, IL, USA) Sheriff’s Office, the championship once again demonstrated how chess can be used as an educational and social tool in correctional facilities. Since the first Intercontinental Championship in 2021, the initiative has expanded across six continents, promoting critical thinking, emotional control, teamwork, and skills that support reintegration into society.

title: Three Chess Houses open simultaneously in Shymkent, Kazakhstan
summary: On October 15, the grand opening of three Chess Houses took place in Shymkent, the third largest city in Kazakhstan by population. The new spaces were established in Abay Park, Metallurgists Park, and the pedestrian alley in the 17th microdistrict. Here, city residents can play chess, train with coaches, and participate in tournaments. The opening ceremony was attended by Timur Turlov, President of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) and KazChess, and Gabit Syzdykbekov, Akim (Mayor) of Shymkent. The locations for the new Chess Houses were not chosen at random. All three facilities are situated in popular public areas where Shymkent residents frequently relax and spend their time. The main idea of the project is to make chess as accessible to the public as possible. There is no longer a need to visit specialized sports schools or chess clubs to play a game or meet fellow enthusiasts, as ideal conditions for this have now been created in parks and alleys. The largest Chess House, covering an area of 223 square meters, is located in Abay Park. Two additional pavilions, each with an area of 81 square meters, were built in Metallurgists Park and the alley in the 17th microdistrict. The latter facility also features a summer terrace. The halls are equipped with specialized chess tables, with capacities accommodating 96 and 48 people simultaneously, respectively. “I am delighted to see the growing interest in chess in our city year after year. In 2024, a Chess House dedicated to veterans and the older generation was opened in Central Park. Today, this noble initiative continues. The new facilities will provide residents with an opportunity to gather, practice chess regularly, and spend their free time productively. Moving forward, we will continue to pay special attention to the development of grassroot sports and the support of talented athletes,” said Gabit Syzdykbekov, Akim of Shymkent. The construction was sponsored by Freedom Holding Corp. through the “Freedom Shapagat” Corporate Fund. The Fund coordinated the project at every stage, from pre-design preparation to the handover of the facilities. Once the facilities are fully operational, Freedom Telecom plans to provide them with internet connectivity. “I clearly see the growing interest in chess in Shymkent year after year. The city has firmly joined the ranks of leaders in terms of the number of tournaments and talented players, especially among children and youth. However, champions do not appear out of nowhere: as global experience shows, major sporting success begin primarily with mass participation and public passion. Therefore, one of FIDE’s main objectives in the coming years is to attract as many people to chess as possible. I consider the simultaneous opening of three Chess Houses a significant step in this direction. I have great hope that in a short time, they will become an integral part of the city’s life. Most importantly, the chess-loving community and the number of champions will grow here, and Shymkent will continue to develop beyond the region as one of the strongest chess centers in Kazakhstan and Central Asia,” said Timur Turlov. Chess advocate and President of the Chess Players Union, Shyngys Nurgalimov, actively participated in developing the design of the central Chess House. The general contractor is “Orda-Stroy Capital” LLP. Immediately following the grand opening, the SHYMKENT CHESS HOUSE BLITZ Challenger 2026 children’s blitz tournament took place in the new Chess Houses, with over a hundred young players participating. The games were held simultaneously across three venues: 60 participants in Abay Park, and 20 chess players each in Metallurgists Park and the alley in the 17th microdistrict. The competition was a nine-round Swiss tournament (time control: 3 minutes + 2 seconds increment per move).

title: Chess in Schools Worldwide: Reach, Structure and Evidence in 100 countries
summary: By George Chitiyo, Ph.D.Tennessee Technological University Chess has a long history in schools, yet the field has lacked a global account of how school chess programs are organized, supported and evaluated. The 2026 FIDE Global Chess in Schools Survey, conducted for the FIDE Chess in Education Commission, was designed to address that gap. This article summarizes the main findings from the global survey and highlights their implications for policy and practice. The Survey and the Scale of School Chess The survey builds on a 2021 FIDE and European Chess Union study of 196 respondents, mostly national federations and predominantly in Europe (Hall & Nash, 2021). Conducted online between October 2025 and June 2026, the 2026 survey asked 33 questions, both closed-ended and open-ended, about program structure, funding, benefits, barriers and evaluation. There were 239 respondents from 100 countries on all five continents, representing national federations, schools, chess-in-schools organizations and other groups. Because respondents chose to take part, the results describe the responding programs rather than all school chess worldwide. School chess reaches a very large number of children. Respondents estimate that close to 30 million children take part in the countries surveyed, about half of them in India. They are taught by more than 145,000 classroom teachers and about 22,500 outside or independent coaches. These figures rest mostly on respondents’ own estimates, so they give a sense of scale rather than an exact count. How Programs Are Structured Around the World  Three markers offer a useful way to judge how established a program is: whether instructors need a formal qualification; whether there is a written curriculum that sets out what children should learn; and whether the program uses chess software or online platforms. Comparing these markers across continents reveals two clear patterns. First, technology use is more widespread than formal teaching structures such as a written curriculum. On every continent except Oceania, where the two respondents reported none of the three markers, software use was the most common (tied with qualifications in Asia), and a written curriculum was the least common. The gap was widest in Europe, where 69.2% of programs use software but only 35.9% have a written curriculum. Second, no continent leads on every measure. Asia had the highest share of programs requiring instructor qualifications (65.3%) and using a written curriculum (49.3%), while the Americas led on software use (71.9%). Africa’s results deserve particular attention. Africa had more countries in the survey than any other continent (26) and more respondents than Europe. Nearly half of African programs (47.3%) require instructor qualifications, close to the Americas (48.4%) and Europe (52.5%). The share with a written curriculum (36.4%) is on par with Europe’s (35.9%). More than half of African programs (54.5%) use software, and a quarter (25%) report that chess is part of the official school curriculum, nationally or in some regions. Africa also leads all continents in deliberate efforts to include girls: 42.2% of African programs run specific initiatives for girls, and only 4.4% report that they do not actively promote girls’ participation. Differences by type of organization were smaller. Between 51.8% and 55.8% of each group required instructor qualifications. Chess-in-schools organizations were the most likely to have a written curriculum (55.6%) and schools the least likely (35%). Program maturity, therefore, has several dimensions, and a program can be strong in one area while lagging in another. The results also suggest that easy access to digital tools has not yet been matched by shared, written plans for what children should learn. Without such plans, it is hard to say what success looks like, and harder still to measure it. The Chitiyo-Atkins Model of Chess Program Development When respondents described their programs in their own words, a consistent pattern emerged: programs tend to reach the same milestones and in the same order. The Chitiyo-Atkins Model organizes these milestones into four stages of development. The model was built from the data rather than imposed on it, and it draws on the accounts of close to 90 countries whose responses gave enough detail to be classified. First move. An individual teacher, a single school or a newly founded federation makes a start, often from nothing. A first club is formed, first lessons are taught, and awareness campaigns begin. Activity depends on one or a few committed champions, and there are no formal structures, trained instructors or dedicated resources yet. Building foundations. The program invests in its two basic foundations: people and equipment. Teacher training and certification courses begin, chess sets and kits are distributed to schools, the first structured classes appear and the first school competitions are organized. Reach grows, but delivery still depends on projects and can falter if key individuals or funding are lost. Scaling and systematizing. Chess becomes a system rather than a project. Programs adopt structured or age-based curricula, hold regular regional and national school competitions, use digital platforms and online teacher courses, and build networks of coordinators and certified instructors. The program is sustained by organizations and routines rather than individuals, but it still lacks formal government status. Policy integration. Chess gains formal status in the education system. Signs of this stage include a dedicated government budget line, a formal partnership with or endorsement from the education ministry, chess as a required or elective subject in the official curriculum, accredited teacher courses, and national coordination and monitoring. The program no longer depends on any single champion. The model describes where programs are; it does not judge them or rank countries against one another. Progress is also not guaranteed, as programs can stall or regress when support ends. The model is most useful as a guide, showing each country what the next step usually looks like and where help could make the biggest difference. Common Barriers to Growth Programs at every stage and on every continent face many of the same obstacles. Funding is the most common: 79% of respondents named it among the biggest barriers. title: Finals set at the 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners
summary: Armenia – Mexico 1(men’s section), India 1 – Mexico (women’s section) and India 1 – Serbia (youth section) are set to clash in the finals for the titles. The 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners continued on 14 October with an exciting Championship Round (quarterfinals), bringing together the best teams from Day 1. This stage featured two round-robin groups in each section, with the winners advancing to the finals. Let’s take a look at how the action unfolded on the second day across all three sections. Men’s Section Armenia triumphed in Group A, a 16-team round-robin, scoring match victories against their main rivals – Mongolia 1, Mongolia 2, and India 1 – to secure a spot in the finals. Mongolia 1 had a good run but finished just one point behind. Group B saw the tightest contest of all the quarterfinals. Serbia 2 and Mexico 1 both finished with 10 match points and shared the top position, with the Mexican squad edging out their main rivals on tiebreaks. Women’s Section The six-team round-robin in Group A developed into an exciting race between India 1 and Ukraine. The leaders locked horns in the penultimate round, with India scoring a narrow victory and securing a place in the finals. Group B featured only two teams – Mexico and USA (KS – Topeka) – which played two matches against each other. Mexico convincingly won both, cruising into the finals. Youth Section It all came down to the final round in Group A as India 1 faced Malawi 2, with both teams entering the match with a perfect score. India 1 pulled off a hard-fought victory thanks to wins on boards one and four, battling their way into the final.  Serbia was unstoppable in Group B, winning all their matches, including a crucial victory over their main rival, Ecuador 3, which finished second. The action will continue on October 15, with the champions to be decided across all three sections. Finals pairings: Men’s section: Armenia – Mexico 1 (16:00 CEST) Women’s section: India 1 – Mexico (16:00 CEST) Youth section: India 1 – Serbia (12:00 CEST)

title: Rafael Vaganian turns 75: Decades among the chess elite
summary:
Rafael Vaganian was born on 15 October 1951 in Yerevan, at that time the capital of the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic. His father, a physicist by profession, was a keen chess player and taught his son the game when he was five years old.

At the age of 15, he defeated former world champion Max Euwe in a simultaneous exhibition:

At 16, Vaganian became Soviet school champion, and at 18 he won an international youth tournament in Groningen, finishing level on points with Germany's Karl-Heinz Maeder and Hungary's Zoltan Ribli. At the time, Vaganian, together with the equally aged Anatoly Karpov and the prematurely deceased Mikhail Steinberg, was regarded as one of the greatest chess talents in the USSR.

In November 1970, Vaganian made his debut in the USSR Championships. After winning a strong grandmaster tournament in Vrnjacka Banja in 1971, ahead of, among others, Leonid Stein, Ljubomir Ljubojevic and Borislav Ivkov, FIDE awarded the 20-year-old Vaganian the grandmaster title directly, without his having previously held the title of international master. Vaganian was the first Armenian to receive this distinction. For decades afterwards, he was Armenia's strongest player.

In the consistently strong USSR Championships, Vaganian achieved several high finishes, including joint 3 rd -5 th in 1974, joint 2 nd -5 th in 1975 and joint 3 rd -4 th in 1982/83. In 1989, he finally won the USSR Championship.

Over the course of his career, Vaganian won countless tournaments, including Rome 1977, São Paulo 1977, Kirovakan 1978, Las Palmas 1979, Manila 1981, Moscow 1982, Hastings 1982/83, Tallinn 1983 and Lvov 1984.

Rafael Vaganian in 1984

He also won in Næstved in 1985, Sochi in 1986, Marseille in 1987, Leningrad in 1987, Esbjerg in 1988, Copenhagen in 1988, Toronto in 1990, Moscow in 1991, Ter Apel in 1992, Neu-Isenburg in 1992, Reggio Emilia in 1991, Ter Apel in 1993, Haarlem in 1993, Long Beach in 1994, Reggio Emilia in 1994/95 and Moscow in 1995 at the Aeroflot Open. Vaganian also achieved podium finishes or at least high placings in many other strong tournaments.

Vaganian's greatest tournament success was winning the 1985 Interzonal in Biel. At the subsequent Candidates Tournament in Montpellier, he finished joint first with Artur Yusupov and Andrei Sokolov, who had the same score, and reached the knockout stage of the Candidates matches for the World Championship, but was eliminated in the first round by Andrei Sokolov.

In the next World Championship cycle, Vaganian again qualified for the Candidates matches, but this time, in Saint John in 1988, he was eliminated by Lajos Portisch. A few days later at the same venue, he finished runner-up in the World Blitz Championship after losing to Mikhail Tal in the final match.

In the 1984 revival of the USSR v. Rest of the World match, Vaganian was selected for the Soviet team, but lost 1½-2½ to Zoltan Ribli on board five.

From 1984 to 1986, Vaganian was among the world's very best players, with a peak rating of 2645 in January 1986. This placed him fourth in the world rankings behind Kasparov, Karpov and Timman.

In 1994, Vaganian won the World Open in Philadelphia, and in 2004 he finished level on points with winner Sergei Rublevsky at the Aeroflot Open in Moscow.

His debut for the Soviet team at the Chess Olympiads came in Buenos Aires in 1978. The Soviet team was pushed into second place by Hungary and, unusually, won only silver. In 1984 and 1986, Vaganian won the gold medal with the Soviet team. In Thessaloniki in 1984, Vaganian was also the second-best player in the tournament by performance rating, behind John Nunn, and additionally won the individual gold medal on board three. From 1992 to 2004, Vaganian played for the team of independent Armenia, winning team bronze in 1992 and 2004, as well as individual gold on board three in 2004.

In addition, Vaganian won a number of team and individual medals with the Soviet team and later with Armenia at World Team Championships and European Team Championships.

Vaganian also took part in a number of national team championships. For many years, he played for Spartak Moscow in the Soviet team championships, later in Armenia for Bank King Yerevan in the Armenian championships, as well as in the Netherlands for Breda and for several years in the Russian Championship for Yekaterinburg. Vaganian also made a number of appearances in the Belgian and French leagues.

With Hou Yifan in Biel | Photo: Biel Chess Festival

From 1990, Vaganian played for SG Porz in the Bundesliga, winning a total of six championship titles with the club up to 2007. In 1996/97, Vaganian achieved the best result ever recorded by a player in a single Bundesliga season, scoring 14½ points from 15 games. From 1992, Rafael Vaganian and his family also lived in Porz for many years.

In 2016, Vaganian won the silver medal with the Armenian team at the World Senior Team Championship. In 2019, he received the gold medal at the World Senior Championship in the 65+ category.

Photo: FIDE

Since 2016, Vaganian has been the director of the Shengavit Youth Chess School in Yerevan.

Photo: Armchess

Vaganian has never been able to leave chess behind. Most recently, he has continued to take part in online tournaments, although not quite as successfully as in the past.

Vaganian also remains closely connected to Germany. Last year, he was a co-commentator at the Sparkassen Chess Meeting alongside Artur Yusupov in Dortmund.

Photo: Sparkassen Chess Meeting (Dortmund Chess Festival)

title: US Championships: Woodward takes down Caruana, Lee widens the gap
summary:
Woodward's biggest win of his career

The fifth round of the US Chess Championship in Saint Louis saw 16-year-old Andy Woodward defeat defending champion Fabiano Caruana to join Wesley So in the lead. Woodward and So now share first place on 3½/5, half a point ahead of Caruana, Awonder Liang and Jeffery Xiong. Four of the six games ended decisively, with Xiong, Ray Robson and Abhimanyu Mishra also collecting full points.

Woodward's victory over Caruana was clearly the most significant result of the round. Playing white against the five-time US champion, the teenager obtained a favourable position out of a Ragozin Defence and gradually increased his advantage. In a strategically complex middlegame, Woodward made effective use of the bishop pair, restricting his opponent's activity while steadily improving the placement of his pieces.

Caruana, who entered the round tied for first place with So, struggled to generate sufficient counterplay. Woodward maintained the pressure and eventually converted his positional advantage, despite the fact that his technique was not entirely flawless. The victory was his first against a player of Caruana's standing and arguably the most significant result of his career so far.

Woodward, who became a grandmaster at the age of 13, has already enjoyed considerable success in 2026. Earlier in the year, he won the Challengers tournament in Wijk aan Zee, having previously claimed the US Junior Championship in 2025. His performance in Saint Louis has continued that progress, with three victories and two draws in the first five rounds.

Woodward 1-0 Caruana

Annotations by Johannes Fischer

So, meanwhile, retained a share of first place after drawing his encounter against Grigoriy Oparin with the black pieces. The three-time US champion successfully defended a Berlin Defence endgame to remain unbeaten, although he has now drawn three consecutive games after starting the tournament with two victories.

Xiong moved into the chasing group by defeating Levon Aronian with the black pieces. Aronian temporarily sacrificed a piece in the middlegame, expecting to recover the material, but failed to find the correct continuation. Xiong took advantage of the mistake and retained his extra material, eventually securing his third victory of the tournament.

The result was particularly notable for Xiong, who had never previously defeated Aronian. He has yet to draw a game in Saint Louis, having alternated three victories with two defeats. After losing to So and Sam Shankland in consecutive rounds, he has now bounced back with wins against Liang and Aronian, moving to 3/5.

Robson also scored an important victory, defeating Hans Niemann in a rook endgame. The position featured equal material, but Robson managed to create an outside passed pawn on the queenside. This proved decisive, as Niemann was unable to contain the pawn while maintaining a satisfactory defensive position.

The longest game of the round was Mishra's encounter against Sam Sevian. The 17-year-old eventually secured his first victory of the tournament after more than 100 moves. In an unusual ending featuring a rook and pawn against a bishop, Mishra had to overcome considerable technical difficulties before finding the breakthrough required to convert his material advantage.

The remaining draw was recorded between Liang and Shankland. The latter employed the Dragon variation of the Sicilian Defence, but the position eventually simplified into a balanced endgame. Liang thus remains half a point behind the leaders, while Shankland stands on 2½/5.

Ray Robson and Abhimanyu Mishra both scored their first wins of the event on Wednesday | Photos: Lennart Ootes

Round 5 results

Standings after round 5

All games

Women's: Lee a full point ahead

Alice Lee strengthened her position at the top of the US Women's Championship by defeating Tatev Abrahamyan with the black pieces in round five. The 17-year-old has now won four consecutive games after drawing her opening encounter, reaching 4½/5 and establishing a full-point lead over her nearest rivals. Rachael Li, Megan Paragua and Thalia Cervantes share second place on 3½/5.

Four of the six games ended decisively, with Lee, Li, Paragua and Rose Atwell all scoring victories. The most notable results included Lee's continued winning streak and Atwell's victory over defending champion Carissa Yip, who has now lost three games in the tournament.

Lee's encounter against Abrahamyan was not straightforward. Playing black, the tournament leader faced a tense middlegame in which her opponent initially defended accurately. The position eventually simplified into an endgame in which Lee had an extra pawn, although Abrahamyan retained sufficient defensive resources to maintain the balance.

However, an inaccurate decision by Abrahamyan allowed Lee to consolidate her material advantage.

Lee's performance is particularly notable given her difficult start to the championship. She escaped with a draw from a losing position against Yip in round one and subsequently recovered from inferior positions to secure victories.

The most striking game of the fifth round was Atwell's victory over Yip. The two players, who represented the United States at the recent Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, reached a complicated middlegame in which Atwell obtained attacking chances against the defending champion.

Atwell eventually sacrificed the exchange, giving up a rook for a minor piece to undermine her opponent's position. Although other continuations also offered winning chances, the sacrifice was effective in creating threats that Yip could not adequately meet.

Atwell maintained the initiative and converted her advantage to collect her first victory of the tournament.

Yip, a four-time US women's champion, entered the tournament as the top seed but has collected only one point from five games, with two draws and three losses. She now shares last place in the standings.

Paragua also returned to winning ways after her fourth-round defeat against Lee. The 13-year-old defeated Nazi Paikidze, making effective use of a positional advantage obtained from the Exchange Variation of the Caro-Kann Defence.

Li joined Paragua and Cervantes on 3½ points by defeating Jennifer Yu with the white pieces. Yu encountered difficulties shortly after the opening and failed to find a satisfactory way to deal with her opponent's threats. Li exploited the resulting weaknesses and converted her advantage without allowing significant counterplay.

The remaining two encounters ended drawn. Eight-time US women's champion Irina Krush split the point with Cervantes, who maintained her unbeaten record and remains among the closest challengers. Anna Zatonskih and Anna Sargsyan also drew, leaving Zatonskih and Krush on 3/5.

title: Atyrau Masters: Top two seeds defeated in opening rounds
summary:
Early upsets

The Atyrau Open 2026 is taking place in Kazakhstan from 12 to 20 October as the third stage of the Kazakhstan Chess Cup . The competition features two sections, Masters and Open, with a combined guaranteed prize fund of approximately US$100,000.

Both tournaments are played over nine rounds using the Swiss system, with a time control of 90 minutes for the game and a 30-second increment from move one. The regulations stipulate that draws cannot be offered before move 30, while games are broadcast with a 15-minute delay as part of the tournament's fair-play measures. The ninth and final round is scheduled for Tuesday 20 October.

Organised by the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, with support from the country's Ministry of Tourism and Sports and the Atyrau Region Department of Physical Culture and Sports, the event is being held at the transcontinental city, located at the mouth of the Ural River on the Caspian Sea, between Europe and Asia.

The Atyrau Bridge crosses the Ural River | Photo: Zhanna Lorde via Wikimedia Commons

The Masters section has attracted grandmasters from several countries, including Uzbekistan, India, France, Bulgaria, Georgia and Iran. The top seed is Uzbekistan's Shamsiddin Vokhidov (2649), followed by Indian grandmasters Leon Luke Mendonca (2629), Aditya Mittal (2621) and Pranav Anand (2606).

The remaining players in the top ten of the starting list are Maxim Matlakov (2596), Gata Kamsky (2592), Arkadij Naiditsch (2580), Baadur Jobava (2572), Bardiya Daneshvar (2571) and Ivan Zemlyanskii (2563). Kamsky, a former World Championship challenger, now represents France, while Naiditsch plays under the Bulgarian flag.

The Masters tournament offers a substantial prize fund of its own, with 9 million Kazakhstani tenge allocated to the winner, approximately US$20,000. Additional prizes are available for leading female players, Kazakhstani participants and competitors in rating categories.

Gata Kamsky | Photo: Kazakhstan Chess Federation

The first two rounds produced notable surprises, with the highest-rated player in each round suffering defeat against an opponent rated more than 150 Elo points lower.

In round one, Vietnamese GM Nguyen Duc Hoa (2405) defeated top seed Shamsiddin Vokhidov (2649), overcoming a rating deficit of 244 points. The Uzbek player reached an objectively drawn endgame with opposite-coloured bishops and equal material, but subsequently made an error that allowed his opponent to secure the full point.

Another upset followed in round two, when Armenian IM Sergey Sklokin-Bagiyan (2477) defeated second seed Leon Luke Mendonca (2629). The Indian grandmaster had survived a clearly inferior middlegame position and managed to restore equality. However, he badly misjudged a simplification, allowing White to get a new queen by force.

Two players started the event with three wins in as many rounds and are now tied for first place: Pranav Anand , the 4 th seed from India, and Khagan Ahmad , the 18 th seed from Azerbaijan. Ahmad defeated the aforementioned Sklokin-Bagiyan in round three.

A group of thirteen players stands a half point back. With six rounds remaining, the leading contenders will have opportunities to recover from their early setbacks.

title: Young British prodigies
summary:
His achievement also surpasses the new British champion GM Shreyas Royal's mark of 13 years seven months. Supratit's mother Pooja described his journey:

“Starting in Glasgow with limited coaching, guidance, resources and opportunities, Supratit's journey to becoming the UK's youngest International Master has been one of perseverance, hard work and family sacrifice. With parents who had little knowledge of chess or its competitive pathways, much of the journey after moving to London was experimental — navigating an unfamiliar chess world and finding the right direction with little guidance.

“Balancing chess training and tournaments with 11+ exams, homework, academics and catching up on missed classes has been a constant challenge. Over time, well-wishers from the chess fraternity, supportive clubs, dedicated coaches, the ECF and Chess Trusts joined the journey, generously offering encouragement and support that made a real difference.

“Through it all, Supratit's determination, clear goals and positivity have kept him moving forward with a smile. We are immensely proud of how far he has come — and this is just the beginning.”

Supratit's achievement was formally ratified at a meeting of the FIDE Council in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on September 27, with the decision announced on October 7. The youngster, who represents England internationally, earned the title after securing the required three International Master norms and surpassing the 2400 rating threshold.

Picture: In 2026, Supratit was invited to attend training camps organised by the Kasparov Chess Foundation. “That was an amazing experience, especially getting the opportunity to talk to one of the greatest players in chess history,” Supratit says.

Supratit has impressed on the international circuit with performances against experienced grandmasters and international masters. He secured an IM norm at the 2025 British Chess Championships and has continued to make rapid progress while balancing competitive chess with his school commitments.

The English Chess Federation congratulates Supratit, his family, coaches and everyone who has supported him on this outstanding achievement. A spokesperson for the federation said: “Supratit's skill and hard work are paying off with the honour of this title. He has a wonderful future ahead of him in the game. We wish him well and hope he continues to power up the rankings.”

title: 6th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners kicks off with record 140 teams
summary:
Press release by FIDE

The 6 th Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners kicked off on October 13, bringing together incarcerated players from around the world for three days of international online competition.

This year's championship established a new participation record, with 140 teams from 56 countries registered for the event. The championship is held in men's, women's and youth sections, with teams competing across multiple groups and time zones. The time control is 10 minutes + 5 seconds increment, starting from move one.

Organised by FIDE and the Cook County (Chicago, IL, USA) Sheriff's Office, the championship demonstrates how chess can be used as an educational and social tool in correctional facilities. Since the first Intercontinental Championship in 2021, the initiative has expanded across six continents, promoting critical thinking, emotional control, teamwork and skills that support reintegration into society.

The opening online ceremony featured FIDE President Timur Turlov and Acting Chair of the FIDE Management Board, Dana Reizniece, who warmly welcomed all the participants. The FIDE President said:

We all know that in chess, one mistake can change the course of a game. But we also know that one mistake does not necessarily decide the final result. There is always another game to play. Life is much more complicated than chess, of course. But perhaps chess can teach us something important about life: our past moves matter, but they do not have to determine every move that follows.

Dana Reizniece said:

You know, a chess game itself is a little bit paradoxical. When you look at the board, it seems to be very restricted or limited. It's only 64 squares, black and white, and the board itself is not too big. But when you start playing, you understand that the game does not have borders, does not have walls, and does not have limits, and it gives us such a sense of freedom and unity. This is something that I hope you experience and feel at this tournament again.

On the first day of the championship, the teams, consisting of four players (with an unlimited number of substitutes), were divided into groups according to their time zones. In the men's competition, each group of eight teams played a round-robin tournament, with the two best squads qualifying for the Championship Stage. In the women's and youth sections, the number of teams in each group varied from four to eight.

After heated battles on the virtual boards on day one, the following teams advanced to the next stage:

Men's section

Group 1: Mongolia 1 and Philippines 3 (Victorias)

Group 2: India 2 and Mongolia 3

Group 3: Mongolia 2 and India 1

Group 4: Ukraine and Serbia 3

Group 5: Serbia 4 and Slovenia

Group 6: Zimbabwe and Malawi 2 (Zomba)

Group 7: Armenia and Romania 2

Group 8: Latvia 1 and England

Group 9: Norway 1 (Froland) and Serbia 2

Group 10: USA – Chicago and Mexico 3

Group 11: Colombia and Dominican Republic

Group 12: Mexico 1 and Argentina

Notably, Mongolia 1, Ukraine, Serbia 4, Armenia, Colombia and Mexico 1 achieved a perfect match score, winning all their day one matches.

Women's section

Group 1: India 1 and Mongolia

Group 2: Malawi and Zimbabwe

Group 3: Ukraine and Georgia 1

Group 4: USA – KS – Topeka and Guyana

India dominated its group, sweeping all its matches, while Ukraine dropped just half a point across twelve games.

Youth section

Group 1: India 1 and India 3

Group 2: Malawi 2 and Serbia

Group 3: Ukraine and Ghana

Group 4: Ecuador 3 and Ecuador 1

Group 5: Ecuador 5 and USA

Malawi 2, Ecuador 3, and Ecuador 5 delivered dominant performances, winning all their matches.

Susan Namangale, Councillor of the FIDE Planning and Development Commission, who visited one of the facilities, shared her impressions of the Malawian teams' results on the first day of the competition:

I am glad that three teams qualified for the quarterfinals, with Bvumbwe Youth finishing in first position in their group, beating Romania, Serbia and Kenya. Zomba finished second, beating all teams and only losing to Zimbabwe in their group, while Kachere Women only lost to Romania, emerging in second position. Thank you, Airtel Malawi, for supporting the event with internet; Ray Cee Tech for subsidising the hiring cost for the laptops; Malawi Prisons Service for the logistics and all support to bring the Mzimba and Kachere teams; all the prison patrons who worked hard; and my team for a good job. I am very proud of building this program from nothing to what it is now.

Malawi is among the countries with the highest number of registered teams, both in Africa and across the globe, demonstrating the growing interest in chess within correctional facilities.

The Championship Round (quarterfinals) promises more tightly contested matches and exciting games. The top two teams from each of the two groups in each section will advance to the finals, while the second-place finishers will play for bronze.
